{{Short description|Topological construction on a map between spaces}}
{{About|a topological construction|the homological-algebraic equivalent| mapping cone (homological algebra)}}
[[File:Mapping cone.svg|thumb|An illustration of a mapping cone; that is, a cone is glued to a space along some [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f \colon X \to Y</math>.]]
In [[mathematics]], especially [[homotopy theory]], the '''mapping cone''' is a construction in [[topology]] analogous to a [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] and denoted <math>C_f</math>. Alternatively, it is also called the '''homotopy cofiber''' and also notated <math>Cf</math>. Its dual, a [[fibration]], is called the [[homotopy fiber|mapping fiber]]. The mapping cone can be understood to be a [[mapping cylinder]] <math>Mf</math> with the initial end of the cylinder collapsed to a point. Mapping cones are frequently applied in the homotopy theory of [[pointed space]]s.

==Definition==
Given a [[continuous function|map]] <math>f\colon X \to Y</math>, the mapping cone <math>C_f</math> is defined to be the quotient space of the [[mapping cylinder]] <math>(X \times I) \sqcup_f Y</math> with respect to the [[equivalence relation]] <math> \forall x,x' \in X, (x, 0) \sim \left(x', 0\right)\,</math>, <math>(x, 1) \sim f(x)</math>. Here <math>I</math> denotes the [[unit interval]] [0,&thinsp;1] with its standard [[Topological space|topology]]. Note that some authors (like [[J. Peter May]]) use the opposite convention, switching 0 and 1.

Visually, one takes the cone on ''X'' (the cylinder <math>X \times I</math> with one end (the 0 end) collapsed to a point), and glues the other end onto ''Y'' via the map ''f'' (the 1 end).

The above is the definition for a map of unpointed spaces; for a map of pointed spaces <math>f\colon (X, x_0) \to (Y, y_0)</math> (so <math>f\colon x_0 \mapsto y_0</math>), one also identifies all of <math>x_0 \times I</math>. Formally, <math>(x_0, t) \sim \left(x_0, t'\right)</math>. Thus one end and the "seam" are all identified with <math>y_0.</math>

=== Example of circle ===
If <math>X</math> is the [[circle]] <math>S^1</math>, the mapping cone  <math>C_f</math> can be considered as the quotient space of the [[disjoint union]] of ''Y'' with the [[disk (mathematics)|disk]] <math>D^2</math> formed by identifying each point ''x'' on the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of <math>D^2</math> to the point <math>f(x)</math> in ''Y''.

Consider, for example, the case where ''Y'' is the disk <math>D^2</math>, and <math>f\colon S^1 \to Y = D^2</math> is the standard [[inclusion map|inclusion]] of the circle <math>S^1</math> as the boundary of <math>D^2</math>. Then the mapping cone <math>C_f</math> is [[homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] to two disks joined on their boundary, which is topologically the [[sphere]] <math>S^2</math>.

=== Double mapping cylinder ===

The mapping cone is a special case of the double [[mapping cylinder]]. This is basically a cylinder <math>X \times I</math> joined on one end to a space <math>Y_1</math> via a [[continuous function|map]]

:<math>f_1: X \to Y_1</math>

and joined on the other end to a space <math>Y_2</math> via a map

:<math>f_2: X \to Y_2</math>

The mapping cone is the degenerate case of the double mapping cylinder (also known as the homotopy pushout), in which one of <math>Y_1, Y_2</math> is a single point.

== Dual construction: the mapping fibre ==
{{main|Homotopy fiber}}
The dual to the mapping cone is the [[homotopy fiber|mapping fibre]] <math>F_f</math>. Given the pointed map <math>f\colon (X, x_0) \to (Y, y_0),</math> one defines the mapping fiber as<ref name=rotman>{{cite book|first=Joseph J.|last=Rotman|authorlink=Joseph J. Rotman|title=An Introduction to Algebraic Topology|year=1988|publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=0-387-96678-1}} See Chapter 11 for proof.</ref>

:<math>F_f = \left\{(x, \omega) \in X \times Y^I : \omega(0) = y_0 \mbox{ and } \omega(1) = f(x)\right\}</math>.

Here, ''I'' is the unit interval and <math>\omega</math> is a continuous path in the space (the [[exponential object]]) <math>Y^I</math>. The mapping fiber is sometimes denoted as <math>Mf</math>; however this conflicts with the same notation for the mapping cylinder.

It is dual to the mapping cone in the sense that the product above is essentially the [[fibered product]] or [[pullback]] <math>X\times_f Y</math> which is dual to the [[pushout]] <math>X\sqcup_f Y</math> used to construct the mapping cone.<ref name=may>{{cite book|first=J. Peter|last=May|authorlink=J. Peter May| url=http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/CONCISE/ConciseRevised.pdf|title= A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology|year=1999|series= Chicago Lectures in Mathematics |isbn=0-226-51183-9}} See Chapter 6.</ref> In this particular case, the duality is essentially that of [[currying]], in that the mapping cone <math>(X\times I)\sqcup_f Y</math> has the curried form <math>X \times_f (I\to Y)</math> where <math>I\to Y</math> is simply an alternate notation for the space <math>Y^I</math> of all continuous maps from the unit interval to <math>Y</math>.  The two variants are related by an [[adjoint functor]].  Observe that the currying preserves the reduced nature of the maps: in the one case, to the tip of the cone, and in the other case, paths to the basepoint.

==Applications==

===CW-complexes===
Attaching a cell.

===Effect on fundamental group===
Given a [[topological space|space]] ''X'' and a loop <math>\alpha\colon S^1 \to X</math> representing an element of the [[fundamental group]] of ''X'', we can form the mapping cone <math>C_\alpha</math>. The effect of this is to make the loop <math>\alpha</math> [[contractible]] in <math>C_\alpha</math>, and therefore the [[equivalence class]] of <math>\alpha</math> in the fundamental group of <math>C_\alpha</math> will be simply the [[identity element]].

Given a [[group presentation]] by generators and relations, one gets a 2-complex with that fundamental group.

=== Homology of a pair ===

The mapping cone lets one interpret the homology of a pair as the reduced homology of the quotient.  Namely, if ''E'' is a [[homology theory]], and <math>i\colon A \to X</math> is a [[cofibration]], then

: <math>E_*(X,A) = E_*(X/A,*) = \tilde E_*(X/A)</math>,

which follows by applying [[excision theorem|excision]] to the mapping cone.<ref name=may/>

==Relation to homotopy (homology) equivalences==

A map <math> f\colon X\rightarrow Y</math> between simply-connected CW complexes is a [[homotopy equivalence]] if and only if its mapping cone is contractible.

More generally, a map is called [[n-connected|''n''-connected]] (as a map) if its mapping cone is ''n''-connected (as a space), plus a little more.<ref>* {{cite book|last=Hatcher|first= Allen|authorlink=Allen Hatcher|url= https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html |title=Algebraic topology|publisher= [[Cambridge University Press]]|location=Cambridge| year=2002|isbn=9780521795401}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=February 2013}}

Let <math> \mathbb{}H_*</math> be a fixed [[homology theory]]. The map <math> f\colon X\rightarrow Y</math> induces [[isomorphism]]s on <math>H_*</math>, if and only if the map <math> \{pt\}\hookrightarrow C_f</math> induces an isomorphism on <math>H_*</math>, i.e., <math>H_*(C_f,pt)=0</math>.

Mapping cones are famously used to construct the long coexact [[Puppe sequence]]s, from which long exact sequences of homotopy and relative homotopy groups can be obtained.<ref name=rotman/>
